turns.prompt_text: The shower in my apartment makes a really loud constant groaning noise when the water is put on full However, this stops if I run the sink water at the same time
turns.response_html:
That constant, loud groaning noise is a classic plumbing phenomenon. The fact that it completely stops when you turn on the sink is the ultimate clue—it confirms that the issue is directly tied to water pressure and restriction within the shower valve or fixture.

Here is a breakdown of exactly what is happening under the hood and how to fix it.

The Diagnostics: Why the Sink Stops the Groan

When water flows through your pipes, it is under constant pressure. If a washer, cartridge, or valve component inside your shower handle becomes loose, worn down, or misaligned, it can act like a reed in a musical instrument.

As high-pressure water forces its way past that loose part, it causes the component to vibrate violently at a high frequency. This vibration echoes through the pipes, creating that loud groaning or humming sound.

  • When the shower is on full: The water pressure hitting that restrictive, loose part is at its peak, causing the loud vibration.
  • When you turn on the sink: You open up a second exit point for the water. This immediately drops the overall water pressure leading to the shower valve and alters the flow rate. Because the pressure drops below the threshold needed to make that loose part vibrate, the noise instantly stops.

The Most Likely Culprits

Because you are in an apartment, you’ll want to look at the easiest, non-invasive fixes first before involving management.

1. A Defective Shower Cartridge (Most Likely)

Inside your single-handle shower faucet is a plastic or brass cartridge that controls the mix of hot and cold water. If the internal gaskets, O-rings, or springs inside this cartridge wear out, they will flap and vibrate under full pressure.

2. A Restrictive or Clogged Showerhead

Sometimes the issue isn't behind the wall at all. If your showerhead has a cheap flow restrictor or is heavily clogged with mineral buildup (calcium/limescale), it creates massive backpressure. This backpressure can force upstream components in the valve to vibrate.

3. Loose Pipe Straps (Water Hammer adjacent)

If the pipes behind your shower wall aren't securely strapped to the wooden studs, the natural turbulence of water under full pressure can cause the physical pipes to rattle and groan against the drywall or framing.

How to Fix It

Here is the step-by-step approach to silencing the groan, starting with the easiest DIY check.

Step 1: The Showerhead Test (Easy DIY)

Before touching any plumbing valves, unscrew your showerhead completely. Turn the shower on full blast through the bare pipe arm.

  • If the groaning stops: The problem is a faulty or mineral-clogged showerhead. Soak it in a bowl of white vinegar overnight to clear the deposits, or replace it with a new one.
  • If it still groans: The issue is definitely inside the main shower valve behind the handle.

Step 2: Call Apartment Maintenance (Recommended)

Since you are renting, this is typically the landlord’s responsibility. Replacing internal valve components carries a risk of leaking behind the wall if done incorrectly.

When you submit the maintenance request, give them the exact details you just shared:

"The shower valve makes a loud, constant groaning noise under full water pressure. The noise stops immediately if the bathroom sink is turned on, indicating a worn-out shower cartridge or loose internal washer vibrating under high pressure."

Plumbers hear that description and instantly know they likely just need to swap out the shower cartridge—a quick 15-minute fix for an experienced maintenance tech.
